items.content: The city existed differently before the sun arrived. Fog had swallowed the sharp edges of buildings, leaving only their pale suggestions floating above the wet pavement, and her footsteps echoed with an intimacy that daylight never allowed. Delivery trucks materialized slowly out of the grey like tired thoughts, and the few figures she passed moved with the quiet purposefulness of people who understood that this hour belonged to no one. She pulled her coat tighter and walked on, feeling briefly invisible, briefly free.

items.content: The train announced itself long before it arrived, a low trembling that seemed to rise from the earth itself rather than from any mechanical thing. She lay still beneath the sheet, listening as the sound swelled and pressed against the glass — something mournful in it, something that spoke of elsewhere, of dark fields rushing past lit windows. Then it was gone, folded back into the silence the way a stone disappears into water, leaving only the faint memory of its passing and the ache of all the places she had never been.

items.content: Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, 'and what is the use of a book,' thought Alice, 'without pictures or conversations?'
items.explanation: Carroll's opening, 1865. The logic-within-illogic (judging books by having pictures OR conversations) is pure Carroll — an eccentric human sensibility that AI replicates awkwardly.
items.source: Lewis Carroll — Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865)

items.content: The world below arranges itself into something almost too orderly from up here — the harbour a crescent of still pewter, the fishing boats nodding like patient animals at their moorings. Beyond the breakwater, the sea stretches outward in shifting panels of blue and green, restless and enormous, indifferent to the small human dramas unfolding at its edges. The wind up here carries salt and distance, and something else harder to name, a feeling that the horizon is not an ending but a threshold, perpetually receding, perpetually promising.
